segments.text: Welcome to lecture nine on vector embeddings for machine learning.
An embedding maps a discrete token into a dense vector of real numbers.
Similar meanings end up close together in the vector space.
We measure closeness with cosine similarity between two vectors.
Cosine similarity ignores magnitude and focuses on the angle between vectors.
Training uses a contrastive objective that pulls positive pairs together.
Negative pairs are pushed apart to spread the representation.
The dimensionality of the embedding controls capacity and cost.
Higher dimensions capture more nuance but require more memory and compute.
For retrieval we store embeddings in an approximate nearest neighbor index.
An ANN index like HNSW trades a little recall for much faster search.
Quantization compresses vectors to reduce storage at a small accuracy cost.
Fine-tuning embeddings on your domain usually beats generic off-the-shelf models.
Evaluate embeddings with recall at k and mean reciprocal rank on a labeled set.
Beware of embedding drift when the underlying model version changes.
Always re-index after upgrading the embedding model to avoid mixed spaces.
Next lecture covers transformer attention and positional encodings.
